title: InvestED, in order: a Rule #1 course
source: InvestED: The Rule #1 Podcast (Phil Town and Danielle Town), https://feeds.megaphone.fm/investedpodcast

modules.title: Orientation
modules.goal: Why Rule #1 investing, who's teaching, and how the course works.
modules.lesson:
1. **Retirement is a numbers problem you can't outsource to hope.** A typical plan is mostly the house plus a fund returning ~6%; after inflation it can run dry in about five years of drawing income, whereas the same savings at 15% changes the outcome ([029](episodes/029.md)).
2. **Compounding works both ways.** Inflation shrinks spending power and salaries lag it; debt compounds against you too ([030](episodes/030.md)).
3. **The best hedge is owning businesses with pricing power:** a moat lets a company raise prices with inflation.
4. **Manage your own money for three reasons:** moral, financial (you should do better) and practical (it isn't rocket science). Investing is a daily practice, like yoga, that you never finish ([065](episodes/065.md)).
5. **Patience is only possible with your own capital.** Fund managers are judged quarterly and can't sit in cash; you can.
6. Rule #1 (don't lose money) still frames everything; the retirement maths is *why* it matters.

modules.title: Understand the business
modules.goal: Circle of competence, the three circles, reading 10-Ks, and investing in line with your values.
modules.lesson:
Munger's four filters run in order, and **understanding** comes first: if you can't understand the business, stop.

1. **Know your why** ([188](episodes/188.md)): own compounding machines (high returns, reinvested) that outrun inflation, and let your money back only companies you would defend.
2. **Find ideas without throwing darts.** Events, great investors' buys and products you use give names, never decisions ([001](episodes/001.md), [011](episodes/011.md), [016](episodes/016.md), [077](episodes/077.md)). Tips are perishable, but don't rush the homework ([190](episodes/190.md)).
3. **Start inside your circles** ([076](episodes/076.md)): overlap what you love, what you're world-class at and where you make and spend money. Radar's gate ([253](episodes/253.md)): two of three circles, a guru holding 4%+ of *their* portfolio (a tip, not urgent) and an industry you know or want to master (mandatory).
4. **Ignorance is the risk.** Circles grow by connection (Harley to Polaris), but your *feeling* of competence outruns your knowledge, and the edge is where money is lost ([078](episodes/078.md), [079](episodes/079.md), [190](episodes/190.md)).
5. **End every project one of three ways** ([190](episodes/190.md)): no, yes at $X (watch list) or the too-hard box. Wait for a fat pitch.
6. **Run the root-canal test:** if reading about the business is fun, you can learn it. Use the product, read its history, then the 10-K ([017](episodes/017.md)).
7. **Research a company you love in order** ([153](episodes/153.md), Stitch Fix): use it, name the competitors, test the moat, check the track record, then rough out a price. No history means too hard.
8. **Concentrate and dig your canyon;** scuttlebutt plus filings beat many names studied lightly ([085](episodes/085.md), [016](episodes/016.md), replayed as [223](episodes/223.md)). A private brand you love can't be bought, but it can point to a listed competitor or retailer.
9. **Run fashionable assets through the same list** (Bitcoin, [135](episodes/135.md)): no understanding or cash flow means speculation.
10. **Respect the edge** ([150](episodes/150.md)): the costliest error is a business you half-understand. Keep the error checklist short, and invert it.
11. **Run the Meaning list** ([254](episodes/254.md), [256](episodes/256.md)): how it makes money in one sentence, top rivals ranked by cash flow, core customer, problem solved, history, how firms in the industry fail, KPIs, the industry in 10 years. A failed sentence is a red flag; a vague label ("mobility company") worries. Keep each list to ten items or fewer.
12. **Stay a student** ([245](episodes/245.md), replaying [047](episodes/047.md)): an inch wide and a mile deep, with a margin of safety for what you don't know.
13. **Next question:** what is the moat, and do the numbers show it?

modules.title: Moats
modules.goal: The five moats (brand, secret, toll bridge, switching, price), how to spot a durable competitive advantage, and how to tell when it's eroding.
modules.lesson:
1. **A moat is an *intrinsic*, *durable* advantage** (Buffett's water around the castle): remove it and the business suffers; rivals with the whole market cap still couldn't win ([003](episodes/003.md)). It is necessary, not sufficient.
2. **Six kinds** ([080](episodes/080.md), [088](episodes/088.md)): brand, toll bridge, price (*lowest cost*, not low price), switching, secrets (patents) and network effect. Earlier notes list five; network effect is a subset of switching. Companies can stack several.
3. **Moats are breachable.** Few companies from 1900 survive, and technology is hard because of creative destruction. Copying erodes them: Whole Foods lost its brand and secret edge once Kroger added organic ranges ([116](episodes/116.md)); USG's brand earns a premium yet overcapacity wrecked returns ([113](episodes/113.md)).
4. **Pricing power is the payoff** ([178](episodes/178.md)): a moat lets a company raise prices when costs rise, so a portfolio of moats resists inflation better than the index. Gold, currency and Bitcoin produce no earnings and can only be speculated on.
5. **Scuttlebutt first:** talk to staff and customers, read the bears and ask competitors why they differ ([080](episodes/080.md)).
6. **Two tests** ([081](episodes/081.md), [082](episodes/082.md)): the numbers (ROE about 10% or better, free cash flow ÷ revenue) and an *obvious* moat. If you must strain to see it, it is too hard. Numbers look out of the back window, and obvious moats are already expensive ([110](episodes/110.md)).
7. **State it in a sentence.** If the 10-K and CEO can't point to the moat, don't invent one ([102](episodes/102.md)). Patagonia's rests on real use by experts, Under Armour's team deals are only marketing ([105](episodes/105.md)).
8. **Replication test:** could you spend the purchase price and build a rival? A moat should survive an idiot, and shouldn't walk out the door with a star ([088](episodes/088.md)).
9. **Three tests of an advantage** ([257](episodes/257.md)): real, durable (looks ahead) and *intrinsic* (looks back: the company isn't itself without it); also hard to copy. Ask whether customers and suppliers *love or need* you; need fades once alternatives appear.
10. **Innovation stack** ([259](episodes/259.md), McKelvey): ten-plus linked differences (Southwest's single aircraft type, cheap airports, batch boarding) are hard to copy, but can be abandoned. Copying is the right default; stacks arise where you can't.
11. **Anti-fragile = moat plus little debt** ([262](episodes/262.md)): prices and earnings still fall, but indebted rivals vanish and the survivor gains customers.

modules.title: Management
modules.goal: Owner-oriented, honest and capable leaders, and how to judge them from letters, calls and capital allocation.
modules.lesson:
1. **Integrity means integrated:** what you see is what you get. Talent is mainly **capital allocation**: reinvest, acquire, pay out or buy back ([005](episodes/005.md), [100](episodes/100.md)). Think like a sole owner.
2. **Management is where you can still lose everything.** A moat protects against an idiot, not a clever bad actor who loads the company with debt ([089](episodes/089.md), [117](episodes/117.md), [127](episodes/127.md)). 
3. **Debt is the real danger** (Horsehead, [075](episodes/075.md)). Years to repay from free cash flow: three at most, and falling ([089](episodes/089.md), [090](episodes/090.md)); [123](episodes/123.md) (replayed as [239](episodes/239.md)) prefers one to two. Borrowing to pay out cash lifts ROE but not ROIC, so a widening gap flags rising debt.
4. **Follow the incentives** ([126](episodes/126.md)): short-tenure bonuses, dilution, reverse splits and voting preferred shares show where owners rank. Pay tied to EPS or options rewards buying stock at any price ([226](episodes/226.md)).
5. **Six warning signs** ([089](episodes/089.md), [102](episodes/102.md)): pay tied to asset size, little own money in the stock, bad acquisitions, shares sold below value, a puff-piece letter, EBITDA treated as cash.
6. **Buybacks and acquisitions pass one test:** buy only below intrinsic value ([100](episodes/100.md), [226](episodes/226.md)). Paying $200 for $100 of value burns owners' money. Rising EPS can hide falling earnings; debt-funded buybacks at high prices are a warning and a character test ([227](episodes/227.md)).
7. **Read the words** ([162](episodes/162.md), [091](episodes/091.md), replayed as [238](episodes/238.md)): great CEOs write candid letters with facts and admitted mistakes. Check old plans against results.
8. **Know who the board answers to** ([148](episodes/148.md), [224](episodes/224.md), [225](episodes/225.md)): shareholders are the legal owners, yet boards often depend on the CEO. Staggered boards and CEO-chosen slates entrench; activists can fix or harm. Read the proxy.
9. **If you can't meet them, use clues** ([126](episodes/126.md), [127](episodes/127.md)): a founder with a big stake, no debt, and great investors buying. If two people decide everything (Sears), it is too hard.
10. **Refinement:** management matters *less* than the business ([053](episodes/053.md)); [123](episodes/123.md) weights it slightly less for mature moats, yet it holds a veto.
11. **Read the cash flow statement as a story** ([208](episodes/208.md)): what was spent, and what would you have done? Judge ROIC on *incremental* capital. Owners' answer to poor allocation is to sell, not to ask for new laws ([227](episodes/227.md)).

modules.title: The numbers: Big Five and ROIC
modules.goal: ROIC, sales, EPS, equity (BVPS) and operating cash flow growth, plus debt, and what they reveal about a moat.
modules.lesson:
1. **ROE (profit ÷ equity) of 10%+ for ten years, not falling, with no debt** is the first proof of a moat ([004](episodes/004.md)). Ten years is long enough for competitors to attack.
2. **Later refinement: ROIC** (return on all invested capital, debt included) is the better number; with no debt, ROE and ROIC match, so Phil simplifies to *avoid debt* ([021](episodes/021.md), [022](episodes/022.md)).
3. **The big four growth rates:** equity (book value) per share, EPS, sales and operating cash flow per share. Look for each at about 10%+ a year and *moving together* ([019](episodes/019.md), [020](episodes/020.md)). Tangled lines (General Motors) mean too hard.
4. **Operating cash flow is the canary** that catches accounting fictions first; EPS is partly a "fiction" of accruals.
5. **Know where each number comes from** ([068](episodes/068.md)): free cash flow isn't a GAAP figure, so two sites can differ. Go to the 10-K and read the notes on odd lines.
6. **The numbers are rear-view.** They show a moat existed; you still must understand why it will last ([023](episodes/023.md)).
7. **Score a real case** ([043](episodes/043.md)): Chipotle against seven numbers. Tech is mostly avoided because moats there erode fast ([022](episodes/022.md)).
8. **Words are data too** ([171](episodes/171.md), [176](episodes/176.md), filed here by the notes; see the management module for [162](episodes/162.md)): Rittenhouse scores CEO letters for candor versus *fog*, counting checkable facts against generalities. A low-fog letter shows an owner of the message, whoever typed it; compare successive CEOs (Home Depot's Blank and Nardelli). Her hub is *capital stewardship*: management that feels *entrusted*, not entitled.

modules.title: Valuation and margin of safety
modules.goal: Sticker Price, the MOS price, Payback Time, Ten Cap and the reasoning behind each.
modules.lesson:
1. **Price is what you pay, value is what you get** ([006](episodes/006.md)). Value is cash that reaches the owner, not accrual "fiction" ([177](episodes/177.md)); compare cash with earnings over ten years ([069](episodes/069.md), [095](episodes/095.md)).
2. **Owner earnings** ([177](episodes/177.md), [181](episodes/181.md), [182](episodes/182.md), [183](episodes/183.md)): net income + depreciation and amortization + change in receivables + change in payables + income tax, less *maintenance* capex. Picture a rented house: rent, minus running costs, minus a roof fund. Operating cash flow ignores maintenance; free cash flow subtracts growth spending too. It is "vaguely right" on purpose, and if you can't finish it you don't understand the business.
3. **Maintenance capex is the art** ([184](episodes/184.md), [186](episodes/186.md)): filings lump it with growth, so read the words ("primarily related to" expansion), use depreciation as a proxy, take the conservative number and stop once more precision can't change the answer. Check third-party capex against the 10-K.
4. **Ten cap** ([146](episodes/146.md), [183](episodes/183.md), [184](episodes/184.md)): owner earnings × 10, a pre-tax 10% yield like a cap rate. It assumes a moat and honest managers. Triangulate with sticker price and payback time: two of three should say on sale.
5. **Sticker price, four inputs** ([009](episodes/009.md), [024](episodes/024.md), [054](episodes/054.md), [121](episodes/121.md)): trailing EPS, ten-year growth, future P/E (lower of twice growth or historical high), 15% MARR. The **windage** growth rate is judgement across 5, 7 and 10 years of the big four. Use the lower of historical and analyst growth ([093](episodes/093.md), [122](episodes/122.md)); analysts' 25% for Fiat Chrysler was absurd ([186](episodes/186.md)).
6. **Buy at half the sticker price** ([010](episodes/010.md), [058](episodes/058.md)), or at most eight years' payback ([008](episodes/008.md), [059](episodes/059.md)). Discounts need a trigger ([121](episodes/121.md)).
7. **Read the gap.** Negative owner earnings, funded by borrowing, flagged Sears years early ([185](episodes/185.md)). A value far above price needs an explanation ([186](episodes/186.md)); too hard is a fine answer.
8. **Reverse-engineer a price:** find the growth it implies ([122](episodes/122.md)). Checklist ([071](episodes/071.md)).
9. **Dividends are not an input** ([066](episodes/066.md)). **Values veto, they don't discount** ([044](episodes/044.md)).
10. **Market-level gauges refine the hunt** ([247](episodes/247.md), [248](episodes/248.md)): Wilshire 5000/GDP (about 80% fair, over 120% a red flag; ~170% in early 2020) and Shiller's CAPE (average 15-16; above 24-25 dangerous) explain why few names pass. They are not timers, and Phil can't say when. A price fall is not a bargain, and buybacks above value spend a dollar on fifty cents.

modules.title: Events and buying
modules.goal: Waiting for a business to go on sale, events, buying in tranches and building a watchlist.
modules.lesson:
1. **Mr. Market is moody; you may ignore him** and buy when fear puts a good business on sale ([007](episodes/007.md)). Volatility is not risk.
2. **An event is a *marvelous* business with a *one-time, solvable* problem** ([025](episodes/025.md), [217](episodes/217.md)): it must recover in about one to three years. IBM's cloud miss may not be solvable; Chipotle's E. coli was fixed, yet the price stayed low for years. A bankruptcy is not an event: shareholders are usually wiped out and trading the stock is gambling ([241](episodes/241.md)). Nor is a slow train wreck of regulation, debt or neglect.
3. **No event, no sale** ([240](episodes/240.md)): if your numbers say cheap at a record high, assume it isn't on sale. Others may know what you don't (a value trap). Ask where the fear and greed are. Google at $200 was Phil's exception; misses are only errors of omission.
4. **System-wide events** (an election, a crash) move price without changing value ([083](episodes/083.md)). Use the fear to see whether watch-list names reach a margin-of-safety price.
5. **RULERS** ([012](episodes/012.md)): Radar, Understand, Love, Event, Reduce basis, Story. Radar has five sources ([077](episodes/077.md)); each gives only a name.
6. **Buy in tranches** as the price falls, and keep cash as an advantage ("1932, not 1999": [199](episodes/199.md)). Be *anti-fragile*. Tranches are dollars, not shares: about four of 25% ([266](episodes/266.md)), so a lower price buys more.
7. **Whole-market gauges** (market cap to GDP, Shiller P/E, rates) say how hard to hunt, not when ([039](episodes/039.md), [147](episodes/147.md), [196](episodes/196.md), [220](episodes/220.md), [205](episodes/205.md)). An index meets "investing" only as a bet on America ([195](episodes/195.md)). Burry's warning that passive money ignores price and thin trading leaves one exit ([232](episodes/232.md)) is an argument with no timing, not a forecast. Bonds are a weak haven at low yields.
8. **Omission is the price of discipline** ([205](episodes/205.md)): a buy price never reached is still correct. A high market is a gift of time, so build a **wish list** with prices now.
9. **Price what you'd own:** the 10 cap, using owner cash ([147](episodes/147.md)).
10. **Invert the story:** write the bear case first. A drop after buying tests whether you understood.
11. **Cash is okay** ([243](episodes/243.md)): judge returns over the whole period, idle years included. Two doubles in four years then four idle years is still about 19% a year. Berkshire's cash pile is a reading, not a rule.
12. **Sharpen the event** ([249](episodes/249.md), [250](episodes/250.md), [255](episodes/255.md), [261](episodes/261.md)): an event needs *fear*, often a problem of about a year that institutions won't wait out. Ask why the other side is selling and name why it is temporary (cotton regrows; coal was a quarter of BNSF). Finish the watch list *before* the event. **Refinement:** [258](episodes/258.md) calls the 2020 crash an event, but [261](episodes/261.md) says it is one only if the *shareholders* survive Chapter 11, dilution and bailout strings.
13. **Down is not cheap** ([255](episodes/255.md), [258](episodes/258.md), [260](episodes/260.md)): debt turns a scare into bankruptcy. Look for little debt, depression-proof demand and pricing power with free cash flow. Stress-test owner earnings ("would it do well in 1931?"). Waiting on valuation differs from selling in fear. No stock tips.
14. **Fear of missing out is the hard part** ([266](episodes/266.md)): losing hurts more than missing a gain, so waiting for a full bear market is no mistake. Selling puts is advanced and not modelled here.

modules.title: Psychology and practice
modules.goal: Fear, greed, patience, the tension signal, inversion and avoiding noise.
modules.lesson:
1. **Know what you don't know.** Use a margin of safety for errors you can't foresee ([047](episodes/047.md)). Simple is not easy ([087](episodes/087.md), [231](episodes/231.md)): the rules are quick to learn, applying them is the work.
2. **Fear drives mass diversification** ([057](episodes/057.md), [206](episodes/206.md)). The middle path is about 10 companies, 5-10% each, never over ~20%.
3. **Volatility is not risk** ([048](episodes/048.md), [035](episodes/035.md), [104](episodes/104.md), [114](episodes/114.md)); the risk questionnaire's idea of risk comes from efficient-market theory. Risk is not knowing what you're doing. A crash is certain, so size for a 50% fall.
4. **Behavioural traps** ([108](episodes/108.md), [115](episodes/115.md)): sunk cost, endowment, loss aversion, anchoring, confirmation bias. Antidotes: a checklist and a "Munger" to argue the other side.
5. **Mistakes are the curriculum** ([201](episodes/201.md), Dalio): the root cause is the hard part. Phil's dead almond orchard was a failure to *invert*.
6. **Build a written process** ([213](episodes/213.md), Einhorn's AREA): numbers before management's story, a pre-mortem, one to three critical concepts, a journal of claims.
7. **Review omissions honestly** ([210](episodes/210.md)): run the four filters on what you knew then. Selling early is the disciplined error ([228](episodes/228.md)).
8. **Investing versus speculating** ([228](episodes/228.md)): know what you own, what it's worth and that it's cheap. Holding indexes or funds you can't value is speculation. Cash is a position when nothing is on sale. Love a company, but detach when the facts change.
9. **Red flags:** "I can't tell what they do" (Madoff), borrowed social proof (Theranos) ([206](episodes/206.md)). Don't copy Buffett blind.
10. **Market fear** ([106](episodes/106.md), [113](episodes/113.md)): gauges say expensive; technical indicators are off-canon ([163](episodes/163.md), [165](episodes/165.md), [166](episodes/166.md)). Contrarians like Burry need a calm mind and patient clients ([231](episodes/231.md)).
11. **Practise before money** ([014](episodes/014.md), [209](episodes/209.md), [218](episodes/218.md)): paper trade, then a *practice share*. Build a 5-15 minute daily habit around what you enjoy; a heroic routine you drop is worse ([231](episodes/231.md), [237](episodes/237.md)). Being "mostly invested" means knowing your emotions and judging advisers; teaching the next generation is how wealth lasts.
12. **Stay attached to the story** ([161](episodes/161.md)). Investing is a head game ([131](episodes/131.md), [149](episodes/149.md)) and a lifelong practice ([155](episodes/155.md)).
13. **Checklists** ([251](episodes/251.md)): short, precise, personal and usable under stress, nested by stage (Gawande). Buffett and Munger never published one. The first list asks how an idea reached you; log every source, rejects included.
14. **Intentions beat resolutions** ([246](episodes/246.md)): treat a rich market as preparation time; sleep and low stress help decisions (their opinion).
15. **The hero's journey** ([244](episodes/244.md)): skeptics and setbacks are normal; perseverance matters, and teaching is the last step.

modules.title: Portfolio and selling
modules.goal: Concentration, position sizing, when the story changes, and when to sell.
modules.lesson:
1. **Rank asset buckets by what they produce:** bonds are low risk and low return; gold and currency are hedges or too-hard bets ([036](episodes/036.md)); commodities have no moat ([037](episodes/037.md)); annuities bet on your lifespan ([031](episodes/031.md)).
2. **Fees, taxes and misaligned incentives** destroy compounding ([015](episodes/015.md)).
3. **Passive versus active** ([130](episodes/130.md), [215](episodes/215.md), [233](episodes/233.md)): index funds (~0.1-0.25%, against ~2% for active in Bogle's argument) suit people who won't do the work; Phil sees the sheer size of passive money as an avalanche risk, so build a watch list you'd buy at 50% off; for a child, a Roth-held index removes emotion. Above a Shiller P/E of 25 a 10% twenty-year return has rarely happened, so "hold" must mean decades. Dollar-cost averaging or cash for drops are fallbacks; learning is the answer.
4. **Why pros can't focus** ([203](episodes/203.md), [204](episodes/204.md)): quarterly benchmarks and nested money reward keeping up. Munger's "focus investing" is a handful of understood positions; pooling "best ideas" rebuilds an index at active fees.
5. **Reduce basis** ([026](episodes/026.md)): dividends return capital until the holding is a growing "equity bond", only as safe as owner cash flow ([028](episodes/028.md), [066](episodes/066.md)).
6. **Wait for the fat pitch** ([124](episodes/124.md)): cash is a position ([072](episodes/072.md)); bring a washtub, not a thimble ([207](episodes/207.md)).
7. **Read the weather, don't forecast it** ([156](episodes/156.md), [157](episodes/157.md), [207](episodes/207.md)): an inverted yield curve has preceded recessions but is no timer; index flows may feed rises and falls. All opinion.
8. **Sell at intrinsic value, or hold compounders** ([158](episodes/158.md), [159](episodes/159.md), [160](episodes/160.md), [204](episodes/204.md)): sell when the story changes, price passes value, or you need velocity. Graham and young Buffett sold at value; size and moats moved Buffett to compounders.
9. **IPOs** ([198](episodes/198.md)): sellers know more than you. Want ten years including a recession; a short record is a small "risky biz" slice; cash-burners are crapshoots.
10. **Shorting and options** ([160](episodes/160.md), [167](episodes/167.md), [168](episodes/168.md), [169](episodes/169.md)): avoided by Buffett and Munger; a collar bounds a gain; learn the business first.
11. **How many stocks?** ([252](episodes/252.md)): about 20 across unrelated industries diversify nearly as well as an index (Phil's unverified chart), a little wider than the ~10 of the psychology module. Calendar-year gains hide earlier losses (a 50% fall needs a 100% gain). A big margin of safety is the defence; a crash can't be rehearsed.

modules.title: The masters
modules.goal: Buffett, Munger, Graham, Pabrai, Spier and others: their ideas and their records.
modules.lesson:
1. **Dhandho** ([013](episodes/013.md)): asymmetric bets, small loss if wrong, large gain if right ([098](episodes/098.md), [099](episodes/099.md)). Size by conviction; diversification is for those who don't know.
2. **Graham to Munger** ([063](episodes/063.md), [141](episodes/141.md), [164](episodes/164.md), [173](episodes/173.md), [174](episodes/174.md), [212](episodes/212.md)): net-nets meant 100-200 bargains; "old Buffett" bought cigar butts, "new Buffett" wonderful companies at fair prices ("all investing is value investing"). Intangibles (American Express) count.
3. **Patience and fees shape behaviour** ([101](episodes/101.md), [120](episodes/120.md), [172](episodes/172.md), [214](episodes/214.md)): funds are marked to market monthly, so institutions can't wait. Pabrai charges no management fee; Buffett closed his partnership in 1969 ([174](episodes/174.md)).
4. **Work alone, from facts** ([174](episodes/174.md), [175](episodes/175.md), [202](episodes/202.md)): finance's "priesthood" jargon (beta, Sharpe) makes investing look harder than it is; it is a learnable skill. Temperament beats IQ. Munger on beating indexes: "we tried to do less."
5. **Berkshire's core competence is picking people** ([214](episodes/214.md)): managers act as owners; "independent" directors on big fees often aren't; ESG forms are self-reported. A moat buys time to adapt, but management must use it.
6. **Build a checklist from other people's errors** ([175](episodes/175.md)): Pabrai's ~150 questions are mostly debt, management and moat.
7. **Don't copy a guru's buy** ([173](episodes/173.md), [212](episodes/212.md)): you miss the exit and the reasoning. Buffett's cash pile and buyback restraint are readings, not statements.
8. **Index funds are for those who won't do the work** ([189](episodes/189.md)). Buffett's quotes ([216](episodes/216.md)): choose the easy hurdle; know what a business owns and who runs it, not every margin; otherwise the too-hard box.
9. **Mistakes are the method** ([200](episodes/200.md), Dalio): goals, notice mistakes, diagnose, fix, persevere. Never be fully certain; Dalio's early-1980s near-ruin was over-certainty.
10. **Buffett the teacher** ([229](episodes/229.md), [230](episodes/230.md)): he joined investing and ethics. Integrity means the same person to everyone; apply the front-page test. Closing his partnership made him a public teacher. Phil's translation: gurus describe the view from the top, beginners need a guide from the bottom.
11. **Using gurus** ([138](episodes/138.md), [143](episodes/143.md), [145](episodes/145.md)): curate a short list, read 13Fs for change (up to 45 days late). Model, don't copy ([086](episodes/086.md)).
12. **Reading Berkshire's 2020 meeting** ([264](episodes/264.md)): no purchases, a ~$137B "Fort Knox" of cash and no buyback because its own intrinsic value had fallen. Berkshire's obligations aren't yours; size your cash buffer to your own job risk. Phil's borrow-and-hoard advice was opinion, not Rule #1.

modules.title: Case studies and interviews
modules.goal: Companies analysed on the show, and guests' stories and lessons.
modules.lesson:
1. **Real assets obey Rule #1** ([033](episodes/033.md)): understand them, find a durable edge, buy after a bust.
2. **Run the filters on a name** ([103](episodes/103.md), [105](episodes/105.md), [154](episodes/154.md)): Under Armour has an okay moat and negative free cash flow; Blue Apron fails in minutes. **Debt kills** (Horsehead, [075](episodes/075.md)). Debt repayable from two years of free cash flow is fine, three the edge, four too much ([187](episodes/187.md)).
3. **Love is not price** ([179](episodes/179.md)): Amazon was a wonderful business, but about $8B of free cash flow against a $1T value was not defensible. A "starter tranche" of an overpriced stock is just a bet the market rises, and becomes dead money if it falls. A real position is 10-20%; a token one is a practice share ([187](episodes/187.md)).
4. **A news-driven price move is not a change in value** ([180](episodes/180.md)): Nike moved on an ad while the business was unchanged. Fashion is less predictable than food.
5. **Whole Foods, start to finish** ([116](episodes/116.md), [118](episodes/118.md), [119](episodes/119.md), [125](episodes/125.md), [191](episodes/191.md), [192](episodes/192.md), [193](episodes/193.md)): a price moat is fragile against a rival that can lose money. A year proves little (the 10-10 rule); judge the *story*, not the price. A CEO's sudden exit is a red flag.
6. **Disruptors fail the tools** ([128](episodes/128.md), [219](episodes/219.md), [221](episodes/221.md), [222](episodes/222.md)): Tesla was too hard to price: vote your values *and* use your brain, and read the short seller's case without shorting. Mergers (Schwab-TD, [242](episodes/242.md)) need a moat, cost or share rationale. Also, and **crypto is speculation** ([133](episodes/133.md), [134](episodes/134.md), [136](episodes/136.md)). Young firms need a pre-IPO history, or sit in a small "risky business" slice ([187](episodes/187.md)).
7. **Teach and defend one stock** ([170](episodes/170.md)); risk tolerance mostly reflects education ([151](episodes/151.md)); money is a vote ([056](episodes/056.md)). Wealth is more than money ([142](episodes/142.md), [194](episodes/194.md)).
8. **Who you are is part of the method** ([197](episodes/197.md), [211](episodes/211.md), [234](episodes/234.md), [235](episodes/235.md), [236](episodes/236.md)): resilience, one step at a time and a values-based budget (sinking funds for future costs) set how much you can invest. Writing exposes gaps in your thinking; sleep and health feed creativity. a 401(k) already makes you an investor; track percentages on a small account and start with $500. Every achiever in Segal's book failed; Buffett credits communication and knowing his strengths.
9. **Amazon valued three ways** ([263](episodes/263.md)): sticker price about $2,200, payback about $1,200 and 10 cap about $440 against a $2,400 price. A wide gap means the price needs growth to continue ("priced for perfection"), so a wonderful business gave no margin of safety. US-listed Chinese shares may be only a VIE contract.
10. **Judge management in a crisis** ([265](episodes/265.md), Dan Heath): upstream prevention over heroics, silos that hide costs, executives cutting their own pay before layoffs, honest communication.

glossary.definition: Don't lose money. Rule #2: don't forget Rule #1 (Buffett).
Meaning (understand it), Moat, Management, Margin of safety: Munger's four filters, applied in order.
The set of businesses you truly understand. Knowing where it ends matters more than how big it is.
Temporary bad news that puts a good business on sale.
Buying far enough below value (Rule #1: 50% of Sticker) that mistakes don't lose you money.
Making the best case against your idea, then rebutting it or walking away.
Buffett's thought experiment: only 20 purchases in a lifetime, so each must count.
Ideas you pass on because you can't understand them well enough.
A durable competitive advantage: brand, secrets, switching, toll bridge or low cost.
Return on equity: profit divided by shareholders' equity. Rule #1 wants 10%+ for ten years.
Return on invested capital: profit on all capital, debt included. Better than ROE once debt is in play.
Equity (book value), EPS, sales and operating cash flow per share, each ideally growing 10%+ together.
Phil's estimate of value today: grow EPS ten years, apply a future P/E, discount at 15%.
Minimum acceptable rate of return: 15% a year in Rule #1.
Years of cash flow needed to earn back the price paid. About eight or fewer is a fair price.
Net earnings minus maintenance capex: the cash an owner could take out.
First-year cash return on purchase price; the price test for real estate and cash-flow businesses.
Graham's moody business partner who quotes a price daily; you may ignore him.
The theory that price already reflects all information. Rule #1 relies on it failing in the short run.
Modern portfolio theory calls price movement risk; Rule #1 says a falling price on unchanged value lowers risk.
Lower the money at risk in a holding by taking cash back, such as dividends.
A business whose cash payout to you grows over time, like a bond whose coupon keeps rising.
Radar, Understand, Love, Event, Reduce basis, Story: Phil's checklist.
A narrow area you study deeply: an inch wide and a mile deep.
Gathering information from customers, employees, suppliers and competitors.
Gujarati for endeavours that create wealth: low-risk, high-uncertainty bets (Pabrai).
Real estate investment trust: a listed company owning property that passes income to shareholders.
A contract paying income for life; essentially a bet on your lifespan that inflation erodes.
Cash generated by running the business; catches accounting fictions first.
Ability to raise prices without losing customers; the inflation hedge.
Valuing a holding at today's quoted price rather than its value.
Cash from operations minus purchase of property and equipment; the cash left for owners. Not a GAAP number, so sources differ.
Years to double ≈ 72 ÷ annual return in percent; also the quick way to discount a future value.
Tangible book value (equity minus goodwill and intangibles): what the business is worth dead. Taught in 060, later dropped as a method.
Graham's very cheap, low-quality company that gives one last puff of profit; Munger steered Buffett to wonderful businesses instead.
The latest four quarters combined; the earnings base for the sticker price.
The pressure on professional managers to match the crowd and show results every quarter, so they cannot wait in cash.
Purchase price minus cash already returned (dividends); shows the risk still outstanding.
Buying something dear in the hope that someone else will pay more; the logic of bubbles.
Investing a fixed sum on a schedule regardless of price; Phil calls it a bet that the market rises.
Buffett's borrowed baseball idea: there are no called strikes, so wait for an obvious opportunity inside the zone you understand.
A moat where the only alternative is far costlier, usually a physical or regulatory monopoly (railroad lines, utilities). Hard to hold without regulation.
Being the lowest-cost producer, so you survive price wars and troughs that shut others down. Matters most in commodity businesses.
How much a stock tends to move relative to the market (1.0 = the market). Modern portfolio theory's measure of risk; Phil ignores it.
Taleb's term for something that gains from shocks. Rule #1 investing needs panics to buy wonderful companies on sale.
Years of free cash flow needed to repay the debt. About three at most, and falling.
Ask whether reading about a business and its industry is fun or a root canal; fun suggests you can learn it.
Earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. Buffett and Munger call it a delusion because it ignores real costs of keeping the business running.
The growth rate you choose by judgement after studying all four growth numbers over 5, 7 and 10 years, not a simple average.
Buffett's image of holding cash for the storm that rains gold: a bucket, not a thimble.
Owning something makes you value it above what you would pay for it, so selling feels like a loss.
Money already spent is gone either way and should not change whether you hold or sell.
Buying a stock trading below a takeover price to collect the gap: speculation with an edge, not Rule #1 investing.
Share classes with unequal votes that give founders or families control; check what voting power you are buying.
Total US stock value divided by GDP; Buffett called 70-80% fine and 100% playing with fire.
Clinging to a price or past view after the facts change; the cure is to recheck your homework.
Quick valuation: free cash flow times 10 (a 10% cash yield) as a rough fair market cap.
Fewer shares, each worth proportionally more; changes nothing by itself but is often used after steep falls and dilution (DryShips).
A stock bought because its assets are worth more than its price; it depends on management realising the value (Sears).
A low-cost fund that copies an index (about 0.1-0.25% a year against 1-2% for active funds); Buffett's advice for those who won't learn to invest.
A ledger shared across many computers so records are hard to change; the technology is investable through companies, a coin is not.
Initial coin offering: a sale of new tokens, often on only a white paper.
Buying for a price rise without a way to value the asset's cash flow (Bitcoin, a Picasso, tulips).
Quarterly report of long US stock holdings by managers with over $100 million; up to 45 days late and silent on cash and shorts.
Borrowing shares, selling them and hoping to buy back cheaper; losses are theoretically unlimited.
A long/short pairing meant to profit whichever way the market moves; hard because it needs two right answers.
A fund holding longs and shorts, so its 13F overstates its exposure.
A tiny position used to force yourself to follow a company while you learn it.
Phil's concentration test: the top five holdings should be at least about half the portfolio.
A tradable right to buy shares at a fixed price before an expiry date; it carries a clock.
Earnings per share divided by price; the inverse of P/E. A 10 cap is a 10% earnings yield.
Cash an owner can take out after maintaining the business: net income + D&A + change in receivables and payables + income tax, less maintenance capex. Preferred to reported or adjusted earnings.
Directors elected in overlapping terms, so only a few seats are up each year; it can entrench weak management.
Annual filing listing what shareholders vote on, including board nominees and executive pay.
Attending to the present moment on purpose; a way to see facts instead of fear and greed.
Automated service that invests your money, usually in broad funds, for a small percentage fee.
Your written case for owning a company: its mission, moat, management and price.
Customers stay because leaving is costly or painful.
How long cash and borrowing can fund a company's losses.
Total market value divided by GDP.
Price divided by the ten-year, inflation-adjusted average of earnings (CAPE).
A calculation from price and volume history used to predict direction; not part of the Buffett-Munger approach.
Present value of the cash a business will generate; the book calls it the sticker price.
Call where management explains results and answers analysts; Phil treats it as best practice alongside the annual report.
Rittenhouse's measure of fact-deficient, obfuscating generalities in management letters.
The 50-day moving average crossing below the 200-day (the golden cross is the reverse).
A price below current assets minus all liabilities; Graham-style bargain.
A company buying and retiring its own shares; Munger favours companies that shrink their share count.
A parent distributing shares of a subsidiary to its holders.
Exchange-traded fund: tracks an index and trades like a stock.
Moving average convergence divergence: a momentum gauge comparing fast and slow moving averages.
Momentum indicator flagging overbought (above 80) and oversold (below 20) readings.
Owning a stock, buying a put and selling a call to bound the outcome.
Right to sell at a set price by a set date.
Right to buy at a set price by a set date.
Cutoff: buy before it to receive the next dividend.
Plain, specific, accountable communication: Rittenhouse's "courage to shine light into dark places".
Managing owners' money as a trustee; "entrusted, not entitled". The hub of Rittenhouse's seven-system model.
Buffett's stance that a buyer who keeps adding capital wants lower prices, as a hamburger buyer does.
The minimum return a fund must beat before its manager takes a share of profits; Pabrai's alternative to an asset-based fee.
Favouring evidence that supports what you already think; the more time you put in, the harder red flags are to see.
Recording sales and expenses when earned or incurred, not when cash moves, so a profitable company can still run out of cash.
Spending needed to keep the business where it is; growth capex raises output. Filings report only the total.
Capital stuck in a stock that must recover its loss before it earns again; cash held for a crash can beat it.
A private certification for socially minded companies that the company pays for; not a legal form.
Restates net income into cash across operating, investing and financing activities; owner earnings draws on the first two.
Money customers owe the company, and money it owes suppliers; a fall in receivables or rise in payables adds cash.
The owner must put in cash to keep the business going, as Sears did for years, funded by borrowing.
Personal exposure to the outcome of your decisions; a small real position sharpens attention.
A small part of the portfolio for companies without a full record, kept small.
A business that reinvests earnings at a high return and compounds faster than inflation.
A fund that invests in other funds, so investors pay two layers of fees; the target of Buffett's 2007 bet.
Sales growth at stores open at least a year; a retail and restaurant measure that transfers between industries.
Don't hold anything for 10 minutes that you wouldn't hold for 10 years.
An investment bought at a price where you expect your money back, so any big win is a bonus (Pabrai).
The rise and fall of lending: credit expands, marginal borrowers get loans, rates rise, refinancing fails and a recession follows. Dalio sees debt ratcheting up across cycles.
Before buying, write the story of how you were wrong; each failure path gets a safeguard trigger that tells you to reassess (Einhorn).
Munger's name for a few well-understood, well-priced businesses instead of hundreds of positions; pooled 'best ideas' just recreate an index.
Long Treasury yields normally exceed short ones; an inversion (short above long) has preceded recessions but is not a timer.
A list of wonderful businesses you know well with a buy price for each, built during a high market so you can act in a crash.
Passing on a great business, or never buying because the price never came down; a Rule #1 investor's expected error, versus losing money on a commission.
Following others' belief instead of checking for yourself, as investors did with Theranos' famous board.
Pressure from quarterly benchmarks and guidance that pushes managers and fund managers to act against long-term value.
Initial public offering; buyers often purchase from insiders who know more, so Phil wants ten years of record or a small 'risky biz' slice.
An owner who buys a large stake to push management or the board to change course; can fix weak managers or harm good ones.
A stock that looks cheap on your numbers but is cheap for a reason, such as information you lack; a no-event bargain at a record high is suspect.
A sharp price rise that forces short sellers to buy back shares, pushing the price higher still.
Repurchasing shares with borrowed money; at prices above value it lifts EPS while destroying owner value and adding leverage.
One hundredth of a percentage point; fund fees are quoted in them (an index fund at about 20 bp versus about 200 bp for active).
How buyers and sellers settle on what something is worth; Burry argues passive money skips it.
US bankruptcy reorganisation in which shareholders are usually wiped out; the stock may keep trading, often with a "Q" on the ticker.
Money set aside regularly for a known future expense, the core of a values-based budget.
When others know something you don't; different from being smarter, and a reason an apparent bargain may not be one.
Joseph Campbell's pattern of call, doubt, mentor, trials and return, applied to the path of a Rule #1 investor.
The test for an event: will the damage pass, or has the business or the shareholders' stake been permanently hurt?
A stretch of about a year when a price is too uncertain for institutions to hold, so they sell and open a discount.
One short checklist per stage of the decision, so each stays usable instead of one long list.
Phil's checklist acronym: Radar, Understand, Love, Event, Story inversion (with Reduce basis as a separate list).
If you can't say how the business makes money in one simple sentence, it is a red flag that it is too hard.
The buyer a business is really built for, who may not be you.
Key performance indicator: the handful of numbers insiders in an industry follow.
Jim McKelvey's term for ten or more interlocking solved problems that give a company a hard-to-copy edge.
Net cash a company loses per month; cash divided by burn is its runway.
Variable interest entity: a contract structure giving US buyers of some Chinese stocks a claim on profits, not ownership.
Fixing the cause of recurring problems rather than rescuing each victim (Dan Heath).
One instalment of a planned position, bought by dollar amount so a lower price buys more shares.
